AWS hikes prices for EC2 Capacity Blocks: What changed

# AWS hikes prices for EC2 Capacity Blocks amid soaring GPU demand

AWS reportedly raised selected EC2 Capacity Block reservation rates twice in 2026. Here is what changed, how Capacity Block billing works, which workloads are exposed, and when On-Demand, Spot, Trainium, or other GPU clouds may be better options.

 iTechGuides Team iTechGuides · August 18, 2026 · 15 min read 

AWS hikes prices for EC2 Capacity Blocks amid soaring GPU demand, but the change is not a blanket EC2 GPU price increase. AWS reportedly raised selected Capacity Block reservation rates by about 15% in January 2026 and about 20% from July 1, 2026. Capacity Blocks are prepaid reservations for scheduled, scarce accelerator capacity.

The distinction matters for cloud architects and FinOps teams. Standard On-Demand and Savings Plans pricing was not included in the reported increases, while customers buying future H100, H200, Blackwell, or other supported accelerator capacity may now pay more for predictable cluster access.

## Key takeaways

- AWS reportedly increased selected EC2 Capacity Block rates by approximately 15% on January 6, 2026, then approximately 20% more for selected offerings effective July 1, 2026.
- Capacity Blocks are prepaid reservations for specified accelerator capacity, not ordinary hourly EC2 pricing; the reservation price is fixed after purchase, according to AWS billing documentation.
- The reported increases affect selected Capacity Block reservation rates for families including P5, P5e, P5en, P4de, P6-B200, and P6-B300, rather than all AWS GPU instances.
- Capacity Blocks can be rational for deadline-sensitive training or inference, but prepaid underutilized time, separate operating-system charges, and the absence of Savings Plan or Reserved Instance discounts can make them expensive.
- On-Demand, Spot, Savings Plans, Trainium, other hyperscalers, and specialist GPU clouds are alternatives, but each trades away some combination of availability, portability, software compatibility, or operational simplicity.

## What changed in AWS EC2 Capacity Block pricing?

AWS changed the price of selected EC2 Capacity Block reservations twice in 2026, according to separate reports. The January event primarily concerned selected P5 offerings, while the July report covered a broader group of Capacity Block reservation rates. These reports should not be summarized as a single increase across all EC2 GPU capacity.

| Date | Reported change | Scope | What it does not establish |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| January 6, 2026 | Approximately 15% | Selected Capacity Blocks, particularly P5/H200-related capacity | It was not a blanket increase to all EC2 GPU On-Demand or Savings Plan rates |
| July 1, 2026 | Approximately 20% | Selected Capacity Block reservation rates, including P6-B300, P6-B200, P5, P5e, P5en, and P4de offerings | It does not mean every instance family or every AWS region received the same increase |

Network World reported the January 6 increase and said AWS attributed the adjustment to expected supply-and-demand patterns. A later Investing.com report carried by Yahoo Finance described an approximately 20% increase effective July 1 for selected reservation rates.

Capacity Block prices are dynamic, so a live quote can differ by instance type, region, start date, duration, and available supply. Check the current AWS Capacity Block pricing page immediately before committing to a reservation.

## What is an EC2 Capacity Block?

An EC2 Capacity Block is an advance reservation that lets a customer search for future accelerator capacity, choose a start date and duration, and reserve a defined number of supported instances. AWS positions Capacity Blocks for GPU workloads lasting days or weeks, including model training, fine-tuning, experimentation, and temporary inference surges.

Capacity Blocks are designed to place instances in closely connected EC2 UltraClusters for demanding machine-learning workloads. The product therefore sells more than access to an individual GPU. A customer is purchasing a scheduled opportunity to obtain a particular cluster size at a particular future time, with placement suited to tightly coupled distributed computing.

AWS’s Capacity Block documentation says that a reservation can start up to eight weeks in the future. A single block can contain up to 64 instances, while an account or organization can reserve up to 256 instances across Capacity Blocks. The exact supported size depends on the instance family and region.

| Capacity Block characteristic | Documented behavior |
| --- | --- |
| Purchase timing | Search for future capacity and select a start date and duration |
| Maximum start horizon | Up to eight weeks in the future |
| Block size | Up to 64 instances, subject to family and regional limits |
| Aggregate limit | Up to 256 instances across Capacity Blocks for an account or organization |
| Cancellation | Reservations generally cannot be canceled |
| Launch behavior | Instances must specifically target the Capacity Block reservation ID |
| On-Demand quota | Capacity Block instances do not count against On-Demand instance limits |
| End of reservation | Instance termination begins at 11:00 a.m. UTC; the block ends at 11:30 a.m. UTC on the final day |

## How does Capacity Block billing work?

Capacity Block billing is an upfront reservation charge determined when the block is purchased. AWS says the reservation price remains fixed after purchase, but the customer pays separately for the operating system used while the instances run. Savings Plans and Reserved Instance discounts do not apply.

- The upfront fee appears in the month when the reservation is purchased.
- There is no additional charge for unused time inside the block, but prepaid unused time still represents wasted capacity.
- Operating-system charges can continue while instances run.
- Storage, data transfer, orchestration, monitoring, checkpointing, and idle time remain part of the total workload cost.
- AWS Cost and Usage Report records can associate the upfront charge and subsequent usage with the reservation ID.

A Capacity Block is therefore not necessarily cheaper because its published accelerator rate appears attractive. A block that is only 60% utilized can cost more per completed training hour than flexible compute, even though the reservation itself does not add a separate fee for unused hours.
